hero.headline: Trump directs $700 million to coal industry under wartime powers
hero.body:
President Trump signed an executive order directing the Department of Defense to enter long-term power purchase agreements with coal plants serving military installations and other critical facilities, marking the latest effort by his administration to revive the struggling coal sector.

The announcement came during a White House ceremony where Trump received a bronze trophy from the Washington Coal Club, an advocacy group with financial ties to the industry. James Grech, CEO of Peabody Energy, the largest coal company in the US, presented the award to Trump, stating: "We stand here today representing the thousands of coalminers across the country to express our deep gratitude to you, sir, for the actions you've taken to support our industry."

The event drew more than a dozen coal executives and miners, along with several Republican lawmakers and cabinet members, including EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin and Interior Secretary Doug Burgess, both known as coal advocates.

"We're going to be buying a lot of coal through the military now," Trump said at the ceremony. "Under our leadership, we're becoming a massive energy exporter. We're lifting up our hard-working American miners like nobody has ever done before."

In addition to the defense department purchases, the Department of Energy announced 175 million dollars in funding for six projects to modernize and extend the operational life of coal-fired power plants serving rural and remote communities in West Virginia, Ohio, North Carolina and Kentucky.

This executive order represents the administration's continued push to support coal production. In September, the White House announced it would open 13.1 million acres of public land to coal mining and allocate 625 million dollars for coal-fired power plants.

The coal industry has faced significant headwinds over recent decades. According to the Energy Information Administration, US coal production in 2023 fell to less than half its 2008 level. Coal plants generated only about 15 percent of US electricity in 2024, down from roughly 50 percent in 2000.

The administration's investment in coal represents a shift away from renewable energy sources and reflects the president's stated priorities regarding energy policy and American economic interests. The strategy signals a commitment to traditional fossil fuel production as a cornerstone of the administration's energy and industrial policy going forward.

cards.headline: Zelensky proposes face-to-face meeting with Putin to end war
cards.teaser: Ukraine's president called for direct negotiations with Russia's leader, citing US attention on Iran.
cards.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has written an open letter directly to Russian President Vladimir Putin calling for face-to-face negotiations to end the war. The letter marks the first time Zelenskyy has publicly addressed Putin directly since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, and includes sweeping criticism of Putin's 26 years in power.

Zelenskyy proposes holding talks in a neutral third country, arguing that only direct engagement between the two leaders can resolve the conflict. The move comes as the United States shifts attention toward Iran, with international observers noting that both sides will need to make compromises for peace.

cards.headline: Israel continues Lebanon operations despite agreed ceasefire
cards.teaser: Israeli Prime Minister ordered strikes on Beirut suburbs as Hezbollah rejected a proposed ceasefire plan.
cards.body:
A ceasefire agreement between Israel and Lebanon was announced by the United States on Wednesday night following fresh diplomatic talks. However, Hezbollah rejected the proposed deal, effectively blocking its implementation.

Despite the rejected ceasefire, Israel has continued military operations in Lebanon. According to the UN peacekeeping mission UNIFIL, at least one peacekeeper was killed and others wounded when they came under mortar fire in southeastern Lebanon during the ongoing conflict.

cards.headline: House passes Ukraine aid bill despite opposition from Republican leadership
cards.body:
The House of Representatives approved legislation Thursday that would provide security assistance to Ukraine and impose sanctions on Russia's economy, defying both former President Donald Trump and Republican leadership who opposed the measure.

The 226-195 vote marks the second major foreign policy break between House Republicans and Trump within a week. On Wednesday, the House had approved a war powers resolution to halt U.S. military action against Iran, signaling growing impatience with the former president's approach to international conflicts.

The Ukraine aid and sanctions bill faced significant resistance from GOP leaders, who warned that the legislation would undermine negotiations they believed could achieve stronger results. Despite their objections, the measure passed with bipartisan support, with enough Republicans breaking ranks to join Democrats in backing the package.

The legislation targets key segments of Russia's economy through new sanctions while providing financial support to Ukraine as it continues its defense against Russian invasion, now more than two years in duration.

Republican leadership had actively lobbied against the bill before the vote, making the defection by House Republicans particularly notable. The strong bipartisan support demonstrated that a significant portion of Congress remains committed to supporting Ukraine despite political pressure from influential figures within the GOP.

The vote reflects divisions within the Republican Party over foreign policy priorities. While Trump and some GOP leaders have questioned the level of U.S. support for Ukraine, many House Republicans voted to prioritize aid to the embattled nation over alignment with Trump's stated position opposing additional assistance.

The measure now advances to the Senate, where its prospects remain uncertain. Senate Democrats have already indicated they want to use spending measures as leverage on other issues, which could complicate the path forward for the Ukraine legislation.

The House vote comes amid broader debates about America's foreign policy direction. Some have suggested the United States has shifted its focus toward concerns about Iran, though the passage of Ukraine aid demonstrates continued congressional commitment to supporting European security alongside other international priorities.

The sanctions component of the bill specifically targets Russian entities and individuals involved in the ongoing conflict. Congressional support for Ukraine remains relatively strong despite the political pressures that have mounted in recent months.

The legislation represents a significant moment in congressional politics, with House Republicans demonstrating a willingness to break with both Trump and their own leadership on a major foreign policy question. The vote underscores the continued backing for Ukraine among substantial portions of both parties in Congress, even as the war enters its third year.

cards.headline: Chinese President Xi Jinping to visit North Korea next week
cards.body:
Chinese President Xi Jinping will travel to North Korea on June 8-9, marking his first visit to the country since 2019. The trip comes just weeks after Xi held separate meetings with the leaders of the United States and Russia, both nations that significantly influence North Korea's foreign policy.

The visit represents a rare diplomatic engagement between Xi and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. Such face-to-face meetings between the two leaders have become increasingly uncommon in recent years.

China has long served as North Korea's most important ally and primary economic supporter. However, the relationship has faced mounting pressure recently. North Korea's growing alliance with Russia has given the isolated nation an alternative partner, potentially reducing its reliance on Beijing. This shift reflects changing dynamics in the region and North Korea's efforts to diversify its diplomatic connections.

The timing of Xi's visit underscores China's position as a major regional power broker. The Chinese leader's decision to travel to Pyongyang signals that Beijing remains committed to maintaining influence over its neighbor, despite North Korea's strengthened ties with Moscow.

The trip takes place against a backdrop of significant regional change in East Asia. Xi's recent meetings with American and Russian leaders demonstrate China's complex diplomatic balancing act in the region. North Korea's foreign policy continues to be heavily shaped by its relationships with these major powers.

As Xi faces an emboldened North Korean dictator, the dynamics of the bilateral relationship have shifted. North Korea's reduced dependence on Chinese support, driven by its partnership with Russia, means Xi must work to preserve Chinese influence during discussions in Pyongyang.

The specific agenda for discussions between Xi and Kim has not been publicly disclosed. Historically, meetings between the two leaders have centered on economic cooperation, regional security issues, and North Korea's nuclear program. These topics are likely to be central to next week's visit as well.

The outcome of the June meeting could shape the trajectory of North Korean diplomacy and its relationships with major powers in the coming months. How Xi and Kim address their bilateral relationship, economic ties, and regional security concerns may have far-reaching implications for stability in East Asia.

The visit also carries symbolic weight in demonstrating continued engagement between Beijing and Pyongyang at the highest levels, even as both nations navigate complex relationships with other world powers and face evolving international pressures.

cards.headline: House panel advances $1.15 trillion defense bill after 14-hour debate
cards.teaser: The House Armed Services Committee passed the fiscal 2027 National Defense Authorization Act late Thursday, sending the nearly $1.15 trillion defense policy bil.
cards.body:
The House Armed Services Committee voted 44-0 Thursday to pass the fiscal 2027 National Defense Authorization Act, a nearly $1.15 trillion defense policy bill. The committee spent 14 hours debating roughly 900 proposed amendments before advancing the measure to the full House.

The annual NDAA sets defense spending priorities and military policy for the Department of Defense, covering weapons systems, personnel decisions, and national security initiatives. The bill now moves to the full House for consideration, with further amendments and reconciliation between chambers likely before it reaches the president's desk.

cards.headline: British military chief warns of dangerous period for UK security
cards.teaser: Chief of the Defence Staff says Russian activities risk crossing critical lines in UK defenses.
cards.body:
Sir Richard Knighton, Chief of the Defence Staff, has warned that the UK faces its most dangerous security period in his career. He told the BBC that Russian incursions into British defences pose a significant threat and risk crossing critical thresholds.

The warning reflects broader tensions between Russia and Western nations. Knighton's assessment underscores the severity of the current threat environment facing Britain and the military's concerns about Russian activity near UK borders.

cards.headline: Sherpa guide found alive on Everest after being missing for six days
cards.teaser: Hillary Dawa Sherpa survived alone on Mount Everest and was rescued while crawling toward base camp.
cards.body:
A Sherpa guide missing on Mount Everest for six days was discovered alive by cleaners as he crawled toward Base Camp. Dawa Sherpa had become separated from his climbing party at higher altitude on the mountain.

The rescue has been described as miraculous given the extreme conditions and length of time he survived alone at high altitude. Funeral rites had already begun for the guide before he was found. Climber Chris Thrall, who was with Dawa Sherpa, recounted the moment they lost contact on the mountain.

cards.headline: Jared Kushner-backed resort plan sparks days of protests in Albania
cards.teaser: A luxury resort project supported by Ivanka Trump's husband has drawn demonstrations and EU concerns.
cards.body:
A planned luxury resort backed by Jared Kushner has triggered sustained protests in Albania. Demonstrators argue the coastal development project would damage a protected environment, while environmental campaigners have voiced opposition to the proposal.

The Albanian government has promoted the project as transformative for the nation, but the resort plan has become contentious among critics concerned about its environmental impact and the influence of foreign investment on the country's development.

cards.headline: Ex-wife of Dubai ruler's nephew held in custody
cards.teaser: Zeynab Javadli had not contacted friends since Tuesday, prosecutors confirmed.
cards.body:
Prosecutors confirmed that Zeynab Javadli, the former wife of a nephew of Dubai's ruler, is in custody. Javadli had not been in contact with any of her friends since Tuesday.

The circumstances surrounding her detention have not been detailed by authorities. The case has drawn attention due to Javadli's connection to Dubai's ruling family through her former marriage.

cards.headline: Australian authorities seize 100,000 illegal cockroaches
cards.teaser: A record bug bust led to the arrest of what officials called a cockroach kingpin.
cards.body:
Australian authorities caught a person with 100,000 illegal insects in what officials described as a record bug bust. The individual, dubbed a cockroach kingpin by investigators, was found in possession of the massive quantity of prohibited cockroaches.

The seizure represents one of the largest illegal insect hauls in Australian history. Authorities have not disclosed the intended use or destination of the insects, though illegal trade in exotic insects has been an ongoing enforcement concern.

cards.headline: New allegations emerge of unsettling behavior by Graham Platner toward women
cards.teaser: Multiple women who dated the political figure have come forward with accounts of disturbing conduct, according to reports.
cards.body:
A New York Times article published Thursday detailed allegations against Graham Platner, the Democratic candidate for US Senate in Maine. According to the report, a Republican operative accused Platner of womanizing, physical misconduct, and making troubling comments about rape.

Platner has rejected the allegations, characterizing them as "politically motivated" and stating that claims of physical abuse are "simply not true."

cards.headline: Nithya Raman closes gap with Karen Bass in Los Angeles mayoral race
cards.teaser: The challenger has narrowed the margin as California continues counting ballots in the mayor election.
cards.body:
Nithya Raman has gained ground on incumbent Karen Bass in the Los Angeles mayoral race, though many ballots remain to be counted. California's uncounted votes could still affect the outcome of the election.

Bass thanked supporters and predicted she would win a second term as mayor. Live results show the race tightening as additional ballots are processed. The uncounted votes represent a significant portion of the total, leaving the final outcome uncertain.

cards.headline: Anthropic co-founder calls for ability to slow artificial intelligence development
cards.teaser: Jack Clark says AI systems could reach a point where they develop without human oversight.
cards.body:
Jack Clark, co-founder of AI company Anthropic, told the BBC that society needs the capability to slow down artificial intelligence advancement. He warned that AI technology could progress to a stage where it develops independently of human input.

Clark made the comments during an interview on BBC's Newsnight program. His statement reflects growing concerns within the technology industry about the pace of AI development and the potential risks of systems that operate beyond human control.

cards.teaser: Ukraine's president wrote an open letter calling for face-to-face negotiations between the two countries.
cards.body:
President Volodymyr Zelensky has written an open letter directly to Vladimir Putin proposing face-to-face negotiations to end the war. The letter, Zelensky's first public written communication to Putin since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, emphasizes that only direct engagement between the two countries can resolve the conflict. Zelensky suggested meeting in a neutral third country.

The diplomatic overture comes as the United States shifts its focus toward Iran. Trump has stated that both sides will need to make compromises to reach a settlement.

cards.headline: Putin announces plans to strengthen Russian air defenses
cards.teaser: The Russian president responded to Ukrainian drone attacks that have struck deep inside Russia.
cards.body:
President Vladimir Putin announced that Russia will strengthen its air defense systems in response to recent Ukrainian drone attacks. The strikes have penetrated deep into Russian territory, disrupting Putin's economic forum in his hometown of St. Petersburg.

The drone attacks underscore Ukraine's expanding capability to strike targets far within Russia using unmanned aerial systems. Putin's statement reflects an escalation in Russia's defensive measures against these attacks.

cards.headline: S&P declines to fast-track SpaceX into benchmark index
cards.teaser: The index provider said it will not change existing rules to allow early entry for the rocket company.
cards.body:
S&P has declined to change its rules to fast-track SpaceX into its benchmark index ahead of the company's initial public offering. This means SpaceX will follow the standard eligibility process like other companies seeking index inclusion.

To be added to major stock indexes, SpaceX must meet established criteria including profitability requirements and waiting periods. When companies are included in indexes, passive investment funds must purchase shares proportionally, typically creating significant demand and driving up stock prices. SpaceX will need to demonstrate sustained profitability and satisfy other technical requirements before becoming eligible.

cards.headline: Nvidia approves all three major memory makers for next-generation chip supply
cards.teaser: The graphics chip company cleared Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron to supply HBM4 memory for its Vera Rubin products.
cards.body:
Nvidia announced that all three leading memory manufacturers have received certification to supply HBM4 memory for its upcoming Vera Rubin chip line. CEO Jensen Huang made the announcement after arriving in Korea, confirming that Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron have all qualified for the next-generation high-bandwidth memory contracts.

The certification marks a shift in Nvidia's supplier strategy for advanced memory components. HBM4 represents the latest generation of specialized memory used in artificial intelligence and high-performance computing chips. Huang stated the company will allocate memory supply prudently among the three approved manufacturers, spreading orders across multiple vendors rather than relying on a single source.

cards.headline: China tightens controls over domestic industries amid global tensions
cards.teaser: Beijing is implementing new policies it describes as necessary for national security that could affect Chinese companies operating overseas.
cards.body:
China is constructing what officials characterize as economic safeguards in response to rising international tensions. The government says the measures are required for national security purposes, though the specific policies were not detailed in available reporting.

The changes could create complications for Chinese companies seeking growth in foreign markets. Beijing's new approach reflects a broader strategy of insulating domestic industries from external pressures while maintaining state control over key economic sectors. How these policies will affect international business operations and cross-border investment remains to be seen as implementation details emerge.

cards.headline: SpaceX lines up retail investors for IPO allocation
cards.teaser: The rocket company is preparing to offer shares to individual investors as part of what would be the largest public offering on record.
cards.body:
SpaceX is arranging for retail investors to participate in its initial public offering, according to reports. The company has told banks it will not adjust its $135 per share IPO price, maintaining the valuation set during earlier planning stages. JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon is personally involved in pitching the offering to investors.

The IPO is expected to be the largest ever recorded, with banks positioned to earn substantial fees from the transaction. The inclusion of retail investors represents an effort to broaden participation beyond institutional buyers. At the planned share price, CEO Elon Musk's net worth could exceed $1 trillion, though analysts have noted risks associated with investing in the space industry.

cards.headline: Anthropic calls for coordinated plan to halt AI development if risks escalate
cards.teaser: The AI company said laboratories need a mechanism to pause work if artificial intelligence reaches a point where it develops without human input.
cards.body:
Anthropic co-founder Jack Clark told BBC Newsnight that AI research facilities need a coordinated framework to slow or stop development if the technology reaches dangerous thresholds. Clark warned that AI could advance to a stage where it improves itself without human intervention, a scenario he described as requiring industry-wide safeguards.

The company urged what it called a global freeze mechanism for AI development, arguing that individual laboratories cannot adequately manage systemic risks on their own. Clark compared the need to a brake pedal that could be applied across the industry. The proposal represents a shift toward viewing AI safety as requiring collective action rather than company-by-company oversight.

cards.headline: British Heart Foundation to close 150 charity shops
cards.teaser: The organization cited an exceptionally difficult trading environment as the reason for the closures.
cards.body:
The British Heart Foundation plans to shut 150 of its charity retail locations across the United Kingdom. The organization said it faces significant trading challenges that have made the shops financially unsustainable.

Charity shops have served as both fundraising vehicles and community fixtures for nonprofit organizations in Britain. The closures will reduce the foundation's retail footprint as it adjusts to changing market conditions. The organization did not specify which locations would be affected or provide a timeline for the shutdowns.

hero.headline: Microsoft AI chief says Anthropic models cost too much for enterprise use
hero.body:
Microsoft's AI leadership has publicly questioned the pricing of Anthropic's AI models, arguing they are too expensive for most businesses to adopt widely. The criticism emerged during Microsoft's Build 2026 developer conference, where the company showcased its own AI infrastructure and strategic partnerships.

The timing is significant as Anthropic moves toward a public offering while reporting extraordinary financial growth. In May, the company announced its annualized revenue had reached $47 billion, a dramatic jump from approximately $9 billion at the end of 2025. As Anthropic prepares for its IPO, co-founder Daniela Amodei has worked to address investor concerns about returns on AI investments.

Microsoft used the Build conference to present its comprehensive AI development strategy across its product portfolio. The company unveiled Project Solara, an Android-based operating system built specifically for AI agents rather than conventional applications. Microsoft also introduced new capabilities for developing AI applications through Microsoft Fabric and its database services, positioning itself as focused on practical, cost-effective AI deployment rather than premium-priced cutting-edge technology.

The pricing dispute reflects deeper divisions within the AI industry over how companies should structure their business models and achieve profitability. Microsoft operates from a position of strength, maintaining partnerships with OpenAI while simultaneously developing its own AI models. This gives the company alternatives to Anthropic's offerings and flexibility in how it advises enterprise customers.

Microsoft's public stance on Anthropic's pricing suggests the company views cost as a significant obstacle to deploying sophisticated AI systems at scale across enterprise clients. By emphasizing its own approach during a major developer conference, Microsoft signaled that it sees cost-effectiveness as a competitive advantage in attracting business customers.

The Build conference itself reinforced Microsoft's broader strategy of positioning Windows as a trustworthy platform for AI development. The company demonstrated how it plans to integrate artificial intelligence throughout its entire product ecosystem, from cloud services to local applications.

This disagreement over pricing is likely to influence how other enterprises evaluate different AI providers as the market continues to develop. As companies decide which AI partners to work with, cost considerations will increasingly weigh against claims of superior capabilities. Microsoft's willingness to publicly criticize competitor pricing may be designed to shape perceptions among decision-makers at large organizations.

The tension between Anthropic's rapid revenue growth and Microsoft's cost concerns highlights a fundamental challenge facing the AI industry: whether premium pricing can be sustained as the technology becomes more widely available and competitive alternatives emerge.

cards.headline: Anthropic revenue reaches $47 billion as company prepares for public offering
cards.teaser: The AI startup reported annualized revenue crossed $47 billion in May as co-founder Daniela Amodei dismissed concerns about returns ahead of the IPO.
cards.body:
Anthropic announced annualized revenue crossed $47 billion in May, up from roughly $9 billion at the end of 2025. The rapid growth comes as the company prepares for a public offering.

Co-founder Daniela Amodei addressed investor doubts about returns on AI investments as the company moves toward its IPO. The growth trajectory faces scrutiny as public market investors evaluate the sustainability of AI business models and profitability timelines.

cards.headline: Mira Murati returns to public view after OpenAI departure
cards.teaser: The former OpenAI executive re-emerged in public settings after stepping away from the company.
cards.body:
Mira Murati made public appearances after leaving her role at OpenAI. Industry observers noted her return to visibility comes as competition intensifies among AI executives.

Murati's re-emergence reflects a shift in strategy for former tech leaders. In the current market environment, maintaining a public profile helps executives signal their continued relevance to investors and potential partners.

cards.headline: Airbnb CEO plans to launch AI research lab
cards.teaser: Brian Chesky announced plans to establish a new artificial intelligence lab at the home rental company.
cards.body:
Airbnb CEO Brian Chesky announced plans to launch an AI lab at the company. The move comes after Chesky previously stated that Airbnb had not partnered with existing large language model providers because the available products weren't ready for the company's needs.

The lab represents Airbnb's strategy to build AI capabilities specifically designed for its travel and hospitality platform, rather than relying on third-party solutions.

cards.headline: Founders Fund launches game show featuring tech executives
cards.teaser: The venture capital firm debuted a show with appearances by Sam Altman, Palmer Luckey, and other technology leaders.
cards.body:
Founders Fund has debuted a new game show bringing together prominent technology executives and investors. The premiere episode featured Sam Altman, Palmer Luckey, and other notable figures in the tech industry, with Mike Solana, the firm's chief marketing officer, serving as moderator.

The venture represents a distinctive media project for the venture capital firm, blending entertainment with business networking to showcase conversations among startup founders and investors in a public format.

cards.headline: Mangrove forests expand after decades of decline
cards.teaser: Coastal mangrove ecosystems are recovering from human activity that destroyed large areas over previous decades.
cards.body:
Mangrove forests are making an unexpected recovery after extensive destruction from human activity. This comeback brings positive outcomes for both coastal communities and climate health, as these ecosystems serve as natural protectors against storms and erosion while storing carbon.

The regrowth marks a significant reversal of the long-term decline caused by development and land conversion. The healing of mangrove forests strengthens coastal resilience and supports the marine species that depend on these vital habitats.

cards.headline: Privacy tool blocks ads across iPhone and Mac applications
cards.teaser: A new software called Filtr removes advertisements from most apps on Apple devices.
cards.body:
Filtr is a new ad-blocking app for iPhones, iPads, and Macs that extends beyond traditional web browsers. The tool can now block ads from loading directly within applications, leveraging features in the latest Apple software.

The app addresses growing user interest in ad-free experiences across Apple's ecosystem. As ad-blocking technology continues to evolve, users increasingly seek ways to reduce tracking and improve app performance by eliminating advertising content.

hero.headline: Dodgers and Diamondbacks players injured in first base collision
hero.teaser: Max Muncy and Ildemaro Vargas both left Thursday's game following a violent collision.
hero.body:
Los Angeles Dodgers third baseman Max Muncy and Arizona Diamondbacks first baseman Ildemaro Vargas both exited Thursday's game after colliding violently at first base. The collision occurred during a play at first base and left both players unable to continue.

Muncy, a veteran infielder for the Dodgers, and Vargas, playing first base for Arizona, were injured on the same play. The incident required both teams to make substitutions, with the severity of the injuries not immediately disclosed after the game.

cards.headline: Texas wins second consecutive softball national championship
cards.teaser: The Longhorns defeated Texas Tech 4-1 to claim back-to-back Women's College World Series titles.
cards.body:
Kayden Henry's home run powered Texas to a 4-1 victory over Texas Tech on Thursday night at the Women's College World Series, securing the Longhorns' second straight national championship.

The win caps off another dominant season for the program, which has established itself among college softball's elite teams with back-to-back titles.

cards.headline: Yankees lose Aaron Judge to rib stress fracture
cards.teaser: The star outfielder will miss time with a stress fracture of his first rib on the right side.
cards.body:
Yankees outfielder Aaron Judge has been sidelined with a stress fracture of the first rib on his right side, the team announced Thursday night. The injury to the 6-foot-7 slugger will keep one of baseball's most productive hitters out of the lineup for an extended period.

Rib stress fractures typically require several weeks of recovery before players can resume baseball activities. The Yankees have not provided a specific timeline for Judge's return to action.

cards.headline: Hurricanes even Stanley Cup Final with overtime win over Golden Knights
cards.teaser: The Carolina Hurricanes defeated the Vegas Golden Knights 4-3 in overtime Thursday night to even the Stanley Cup Final at one game apiece.
cards.body:
Seth Jarvis scored on a power play 3:56 into overtime to lift the Carolina Hurricanes past the Vegas Golden Knights 4-3 in Game 2 of the Stanley Cup Final on Thursday night. The victory evened the series at one game apiece.

The Hurricanes erased a two-goal deficit in the third period before giving up a late tying goal with less than two minutes remaining in regulation. A failed coach's challenge by Vegas on a goaltender interference call shifted momentum back to Carolina and set up the decisive power play in overtime.

cards.headline: WNBA rookie Olivia Miles sets three-point record
cards.teaser: The Lynx guard made eight three-pointers to break the rookie record previously tied by Caitlin Clark.
cards.body:
Minnesota Lynx guard Olivia Miles broke a WNBA rookie record Thursday night, draining eight three-pointers in a game against the Valkyries. The performance surpassed the previous mark that Indiana Fever star Caitlin Clark tied during her 2024 rookie season.

Miles' shooting display highlighted her ability to stretch the floor as a perimeter threat in her first professional campaign.

cards.headline: Caitlin Clark scores 17 points despite illness in Fever win
cards.teaser: The Indiana guard vomited at halftime but returned to help the Fever defeat the Dream 83-71.
cards.body:
Indiana Fever guard Caitlin Clark battled through illness to lead her team to victory Thursday night. Despite vomiting at halftime, Clark returned to the court and finished with 17 points and eight assists as the Fever defeated the Atlanta Dream 83-71 in their Commissioner's Cup opener.

Clark's resilient performance proved crucial in securing the win for Indiana in the in-season tournament's opening game.

cards.headline: Jennifer Kupcho leads after first round of US Women's Open
cards.teaser: The American golfer holds a one-shot advantage after the opening round of the year's second women's major.
cards.body:
Jennifer Kupcho made a strong start to the US Women's Open, golf's second women's major of the year. The American shot a first-round score that put her one shot ahead of the field on Thursday.

Kupcho will carry her one-shot lead into the remaining rounds of the championship as she looks to claim one of golf's most prestigious titles.

hero.headline: Actor James Handy Stabbed to Death at Home, Girlfriend's Son Arrested
hero.body:
Veteran character actor James Handy, 81, was fatally stabbed at his residence in Tarzana, California on Wednesday morning. Police discovered him in the front yard with multiple stab wounds to the chest at approximately 9:30am. He was pronounced dead at the scene.

Michael Gledhill, 44, the son of Handy's girlfriend who lived at the residence, was arrested and charged with murder. Bail was set at 2 million dollars.

According to police reports, a 911 caller stated: "I am the son of man, I just killed the man of sin." When officers arrived, Gledhill told them he was the person they were looking for. The Los Angeles Police Department confirmed that the suspect resided at the location with his mother, who is Handy's girlfriend.

Handy built a steady career as a character actor across film and television spanning several decades. His filmography includes roles in the 2022 action sequel Top Gun: Maverick, the 1995 adventure film Jumanji, and the 2017 superhero film Logan. He also appeared in K-911, as well as numerous television series including Law and Order, NCIS: Los Angeles, and Criminal Minds.

Born in New York City, Handy began his career in 1977 with the television series Ryan's Hope. Top Gun: Maverick, released in 2022, was his most recent film credit. Over his career, he maintained a recognizable presence in Hollywood through supporting roles in both major studio productions and smaller projects.

His death marks a loss for the entertainment community, where he was known for his consistent work as a reliable character performer across multiple generations of film and television.

The circumstances that led to the fatal encounter remain under investigation by the Los Angeles Police Department. Detectives continue to work on establishing the full details of what occurred at the Tarzana residence. The department has not publicly disclosed a motive for the stabbing.

cards.headline: Scott Pelley and Two Other 60 Minutes Correspondents Fired from CBS
cards.teaser: CBS fired longtime correspondent Scott Pelley and two other 60 Minutes journalists, creating upheaval at the news program.
cards.body:
CBS dismissed Scott Pelley, a veteran 60 Minutes correspondent, along with two other journalists from the program. Pelley subsequently accused the network's new executives of instructing him to inject falsehoods and bias into his reporting. He claimed the executives silenced employees and pushed unverified claims, adding that politicians were given a say in interviews.

Pelley stated that 60 Minutes had maintained its position as America's top program for decades because audiences valued its integrity and quality. Nick Bilton, the new chief of 60 Minutes, pledged to maintain editorial independence for the program following the personnel changes.

cards.headline: Scary Movie Earns $7.5 Million in Thursday Previews
cards.teaser: The revived horror comedy franchise opened with preview numbers approaching those of Scream 7.
cards.body:
Scary Movie collected $7.5 million in Thursday night preview screenings, positioning itself competitively in the marketplace. Masters of the Universe earned $4 million during the same preview period.

The sixth installment of the Scary Movie franchise returns after a lengthy absence from theaters. The film aims to capitalize on the ongoing popularity of horror films, though critics have noted that successful jokes are scarce throughout the movie's runtime.

cards.headline: Taylor Swift Releases Song for Toy Story 5
cards.teaser: Swift wrote and produced a track for the upcoming Pixar film, focusing on the character Jessie.
cards.body:
Taylor Swift has unveiled an original song for Toy Story 5 titled "I Knew It, I Knew You." She co-wrote and produced the track alongside longtime collaborator Jack Antonoff. The heartfelt song celebrates Jessie, the cowgirl character from the Pixar franchise.

Swift released the song with minimalist cover art showcasing her natural curls. The track quickly generated buzz among fans and caught the attention of notable figures, including Brittany Mahomes. Pixar's Toy Story 5 is set for theatrical release.

cards.headline: Phoebe Bridgers Performs Phone-Free Concert at Madison Square Garden
cards.teaser: The singer-songwriter held an acoustic show for 18,000 attendees with locked devices and previewed eight new songs.
cards.body:
Phoebe Bridgers held a special acoustic concert at Madison Square Garden where attendees had their phones locked away for the duration of the show. The intimate performance drew roughly 18,000 people, and Bridgers acknowledged the unusual experience during the event, remarking on how strange it felt without devices present.

The singer-songwriter performed eight new songs during the phone-free show. By removing digital distractions, Bridgers created what she described as a living room atmosphere within the massive arena, fostering a direct connection between performer and audience without the mediation of technology.

cards.headline: Florida Georgia Line Reunite at CMA Fest
cards.teaser: Tyler Hubbard and Brian Kelley appeared together at Nissan Stadium, signaling the return of the duo that split in 2022.
cards.body:
Florida Georgia Line made a surprise appearance at CMA Fest in Nashville, marking a reunion for the country duo. Tyler Hubbard and Brian Kelley performed together at Nissan Stadium, their first joint appearance since splitting in 2022.

The duo signaled their return with the performance. Florida Georgia Line had been one of country music's prominent acts before the members pursued separate projects. The CMA Fest appearance suggested the pair may resume working together as a group.

cards.headline: Kate Winslet Surprises Blind Teen With Phone Call After Film Screening Trip
cards.teaser: The Oscar-winning actress called Eryn, who traveled three hours for an accessible cinema screening.
cards.body:
Oscar-winning actress Kate Winslet made a surprise phone call to Eryn, a teenager who has been blind since birth. Eryn had traveled three hours round-trip to attend a film screening at an accessible cinema because no such venue existed in her local area.

Winslet reached out after learning about the dedicated young film fan's extensive journey to watch movies with proper accommodations. The gesture underscored the significant barriers blind and visually impaired audiences face when accessing films in accessible formats.

hero.headline: Senate Republicans defeat Schumer amendment to block anti-weaponization fund
hero.teaser: Senate Republicans blocked an amendment that would have prohibited the Justice Department from establishing a $1.8 billion anti-weaponization fund.
hero.body:
Senate Republicans narrowly blocked a Democratic effort on Thursday to prevent President Trump from establishing a $1.8 billion fund to compensate his allies. The vote on the amendment, sponsored by Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer, came during an extended series of amendment votes on a $70 billion budget reconciliation package designed to fund immigration enforcement agencies.

Schumer's amendment sought to insert language into Republican-backed legislation that would bar the Department of Justice from creating the so-called "anti-weaponization" fund. The measure failed 49-50, with three Republican senators breaking ranks to support the effort alongside all Democrats.

The three Republicans who voted with Democrats were Susan Collins of Maine, Dan Sullivan of Alaska, and Jon Husted of Ohio. All three represent seats considered vulnerable in upcoming midterm elections. Collins is the only Republican senator from a state won by Kamala Harris in 2024, while recent polling showed Husted trailing his Democratic challenger by significant margins.

The amendment vote stretched for hours as senators huddled on the chamber floor to discuss the contentious proposal. The dispute over the fund has exposed deep divisions within the Republican Party, even as the administration had previously indicated it would not move forward with the initiative. However, Schumer insisted that Congress should pass legislation to permanently block the fund from being used.

"Republicans are trusting the word of Todd Blanche, who built a career on lying," Schumer said, referring to the acting attorney general. He noted that Trump had expressed his enthusiasm for the fund just the previous day, calling it "so important." Schumer questioned whether Trump could resist using the fund for personal benefit.

The larger $70 billion bill will fund immigration agencies through 2029. Republicans are using the budget reconciliation process to pass it without Democratic support and avoid the filibuster. The reconciliation rules allow lawmakers to propose amendments before passage.

After Schumer's amendment failed, Republican Senator Thom Tillis proposed alternative language that would have prevented payouts from the anti-weaponization fund and instead directed that money toward Justice Department efforts to combat fraud. "This bill is unpopular. This administration has said they're not moving forward with it. This is an opportunity for us to put it to bed," Tillis said.

Democrats rejected Tillis's proposal. Oregon Senator Jeff Merkley argued that simply replacing one fund with another under the attorney general's control was insufficient. "The way to go is to get rid of these slush funds altogether," Merkley said. Tillis's amendment failed with support from only 11 other Republicans and three Democrats.

The standoff has complicated Republicans' efforts to settle a broader disagreement with Democrats over funding for immigration enforcement agencies, a dispute that previously sparked a 75-day partial shutdown of the Department of Homeland Security.

cards.headline: House panel advances $1.15 trillion defense bill after 14-hour debate
cards.teaser: The House Armed Services Committee passed the fiscal 2027 National Defense Authorization Act late Thursday, sending the nearly $1.15 trillion defense policy bil.
cards.body:
The House Armed Services Committee voted 44-0 Thursday to pass the fiscal 2027 National Defense Authorization Act, a nearly $1.15 trillion defense policy bill. The committee spent 14 hours debating roughly 900 proposed amendments before advancing the measure to the full House.

The annual NDAA sets defense spending priorities and military policy for the Department of Defense, covering weapons systems, personnel decisions, and national security initiatives. The bill now moves to the full House for consideration, with further amendments and reconciliation between chambers likely before it reaches the president's desk.

cards.headline: FCC reviews $3 billion school internet subsidy program over screen time concerns
cards.teaser: The Federal Communications Commission is reviewing a program that subsidizes internet access for schools and libraries, citing concerns over children's screen time and health impacts.
cards.body:
The Federal Communications Commission announced a comprehensive review of the E-Rate program, which distributes $3 billion annually to help schools and libraries access the internet. FCC Chair Brendan Carr initiated the review citing concerns about excessive screen time among children and its potential health effects.

The E-Rate program has long served as a critical funding source enabling educational institutions to build and maintain internet connectivity for students and patrons.

cards.headline: Susan Collins casts 10,000th consecutive Senate vote
cards.teaser: Senator Susan Collins of Maine reached a milestone by casting her 10,000th consecutive Senate vote during a reconciliation package debate.
cards.body:
Senator Susan Collins cast her 10,000th consecutive Senate vote on Thursday night, voting for a Democratic motion to commit the $70 billion budget reconciliation package back to the Judiciary Committee. Collins announced her vote from her desk on the Senate floor.

Collins wore a red dress underneath a blue blazer with bright brass buttons as she reached the voting milestone. The vote came during an extended series of amendments to the reconciliation package focused on immigration enforcement funding.

cards.headline: Deb Haaland wins New Mexico Democratic primary for governor
cards.teaser: Former Interior Secretary Deb Haaland won the Democratic primary for governor of New Mexico and could become the first female Native American governor if elected in November.
cards.body:
Deb Haaland, who served as Interior Secretary in the Biden administration, won the Democratic primary for governor of New Mexico. She now advances to the general election where she will compete for the governorship.

If Haaland wins in November, she would make history as the first female Native American governor in the United States. Haaland previously served as a U.S. Representative from New Mexico before joining the Biden cabinet.

cards.headline: Xavier Becerra advances in California governor race
cards.teaser: Former Health and Human Services Secretary Xavier Becerra secured a spot in November's general election for California governor as two other candidates compete for the second position.
cards.body:
Xavier Becerra, the former Health and Human Services Secretary, advanced to California's November general election in the race to become the state's next governor. Under California's top-two primary system, the two candidates with the most votes, regardless of party affiliation, move forward to the general election regardless of party affiliation.

The race to replace Governor Gavin Newsom continues with other candidates competing for the second spot in the general election. Vote counting in California is expected to take several weeks as election officials process ballots.

cards.headline: Maine Senate candidate Graham Platner denies allegations from past partners
cards.teaser: Maine Democratic Senate candidate Graham Platner disputed parts of a New York Times report detailing claims from former girlfriends about his past behavior.
cards.body:
Graham Platner, a progressive Democrat and oyster farmer running for Maine Senate, has rejected allegations of abusive behavior reported by the New York Times. The article included claims from past girlfriends and a Republican operative who accused him of physical misconduct and making offensive remarks about rape.

Platner characterized the allegations as "politically motivated" and denied the claims of physical abuse. He stated he has not considered withdrawing from the Maine Senate primary race despite the new report.
